328.s: He learned orchestration from Peter and the Wolf and The Nutcracker scores, and they discuss writing for individuals.
328.q: Yeah. I learned that from “Peter and the Wolf.” The orchestration is bad. The melodies are humorous you know, but the orchestration is bad.

328.t: Self-taught and now ready to study orchestration
328.s: Hampton regrets not studying formally and says orchestrating is hearing, with inspiration beyond theory.
328.q: I haven’t. I’m sorry that I didn’t, because I did have some opportunities to study with some really fantastic people. My love for music sometimes overwhelmed my logic. I had the feeling that love for music would do it. But it doesn’t do it. You have to do the work. Your love for music is probably…

Okay. See, the thing is, in the first of those three things, the first thing would actually be composition, because when you do a composition, you don’t have to have an arrangement. You don’t have to have an ensemble. Composition could be for one instrument. It could be for piano. So the…

485.s: Rowe introduces her; she says arranging and composing are the same for her and rarely arranges others' music, with the elephant analogy.
485.q: I think probably because in my case both is the same. I don’t really — as a rule — I don’t arrange somebody else’s music. I have done a few numbers of Lew’s. I’ve done two to the exception, one Dizzy Gillespie one, and another one, Frank Wess was with the band for ten years. It was my gift to him…

993.s: Daley explains his graphic score, how Mingus drew images, and colors marking leads and textures.
993.q: Yeah. Well I didn’t invent that. I mean the graphic scores have been used for years and years and years. Graphic scores are basically an eye concept that many musicians — I mean going back to like Mingus, instead of having an icon like Mingus would just draw a casket and say pass it on. This is…

580.t: Brookmeyer's advice to delay the solo
580.s: Rowe cites Bob Brookmeyer on putting off the solo; Israels finds Brookmeyer full of dichotomies but sees the compositional point.
580.q: Yeah maybe, yeah. I also, I understand his position about that. I find Bobby Brookmeyer a kind of a difficult person because he’s full of dichotomies. He has done extraordinarily beautiful work and some obtuse stuff that I just don’t understand at all.

938.t: Menza's arranging influences and the computer trap
938.s: Menza on how he learned writing from records and scores, his influences, and how computer-written parts ignore breathing.
938.q: It’s cool. As long as they — it doesn’t matter. You know the saxophone parts, it’s nothing, everything that I’ve written I’ve played. It’s all based on my small group concept, all my big band charts. Everything. It’s a mood that I’ve experienced on the bandstand and I’ve translated it to the big…

965.t: Giving every orchestra player a real part; pops orchestra arrangements
965.s: On the bassoon question he talks about writing idiomatic parts for orchestra players, his pops work, and the poor arrangements pops orchestras get.
965.q: Interesting you should choose the bassoon. I love the bassoon. I mean I love the bassoon in the orchestra, it’s a wonderful instrument. I do a lot of orchestral pops arrangements for Cincinnati Pops, Boston Pops and other orchestras and for events where they accompany singers. And I love the…

487.t: Arranging as an inventive process and learning music like a language
487.s: The joy of a blank page and how a lifetime of listening becomes musical vocabulary.
487.q: Yes. You’re right. I mean you know the way I look at it is you’re faced with a blank piece of paper and now you’ve got to put notes, you’ve got to put things on there that are going to sound nice. So it’s a very inventive process. So I still, I’m still just as enthused whenever there’s another…

989.t: Hearing arrangements played and instrument weight
989.s: On the importance of balancing instruments in arranging, and classical composers having orchestras on hand to try their work.
989.q: Yes I mean you know as you gain more knowledge of arranging, orchestration, you know, compositions, one comes to realize that one of the most important things is the weight of the instrument against another instrument. And if you, you know, after trial and error should be able to realize that, you…

153.s: Buddy Baker taught him to give strings plain note values, and Clark Terry's 'No ta-ta, boo-ya' showed students the swing feel.
153.q: When I met Buddy Baker, the first thing he told me, he says, “If you want to write about strings, you’ve got to remember one thing: strings don’t swing.” You can’t write notes for them like you would for saxophones, because they’re not going to play it with that feel. Even if you give them like a…

223.t: Arranging versus composing and studying with Russ Garcia
223.s: A good chart is a composition; his private study with Garcia was informal and centred on form.
223.q: No. Arranging, you‟re working with somebody else‟s composition. A good jazz chart, I think, has got to be a composition of its own. You‟re using – maybe you‟re using a tone row that another composer laid on you, but it‟s composition too. You don‟t get any royalties from it, but if you like what…
